stem: The scores of candidates in a competitive exam follow a normal distribution with mean 72 and standard deviation 8. The passing mark is 80. Using the standard normal table where P(Z < 1) = 0.8413, what is the approximate percentage of candidates who pass?

per_option_rationale.rationale: P(Z < 1) = 0.8413 means 84.13% score below 80, not above; failing to take the complement gives this wrong answer.
34.13% is P(0 < Z < 1), the area in only the right half between the mean and one sigma; it mistakes the one-sided tail for the symmetric sub-region.
50% would be correct only if the passing mark equalled the mean (72), but 80 is one sigma above the mean.

explanation: Standardise: Z = (80 - 72) / 8 = 1. The passing region is X > 80, equivalently Z > 1. From the table P(Z < 1) = 0.8413, so P(Z > 1) = 1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587. The critical move is taking the complement of the table value, because tables give left-tail probabilities.

explanation_sections.punchline: After standardising to Z = 1, the pass rate is the right-tail probability 1 - 0.8413 = 15.87%, not the table value itself.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model (normal) and standardise: Z = (x - mu) / sigma = (80 - 72) / 8 = 1. The table gives P(Z < z); for P(X > 80) = P(Z > 1), apply complement: 1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587. Convert to percentage: 15.87%.
explanation_sections.lesson: Normal table values are always left-tail (cumulative). For 'greater than' questions, subtract from 1.
explanation_sections.timing: About 60-70 seconds. The only trap is using the table value directly instead of taking 1 minus it.
